analysis.one_liner: Requires businesses to be warned and given months to fix accessibility barriers before disabled people can sue under the ADA.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 15-6 in July 2016, but the full House never voted, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Americans with Disabilities Act so a disabled person who finds a business or public building inaccessible could not sue right away. First they would have to send the owner a detailed written notice of the barrier; the owner would then get 60 days to promise a fix in writing and another 120 days to remove it or show 'substantial progress.' The bill would also make it a federal crime to send a demand letter alleging an ADA violation without spelling out exactly how a person was denied access, and would direct the Justice Department to run education programs and push mediation instead of lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of stores, restaurants, and other public accommodations, especially those with inaccessible premises. They would get up to 180 days of protection from being sued, freedom from demand letters that lack detail, and a government program to help them comply voluntarily.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Business and property owners facing ADA suits

how_it_helps.text: A person could not file a civil action over an architectural barrier until they gave the owner a written notice specific enough to identify the barrier, and the owner either failed to respond with a written improvement plan within 60 days or failed to remove the barrier or make 'substantial progress' within 120 days after providing a plan.

It would become a crime, punishable by fine, to send a demand letter alleging an ADA public accommodation violation unless it specifies the address, the exact ADA sections violated, whether assistance was requested, and whether the barrier was permanent or temporary.

The Justice Department's Disability Rights Section would develop a program to educate state and local governments and property owners on access strategies, and the federal courts would develop a model mediation program so barrier claims are resolved without costly litigation.

analysis.who_pays: People with disabilities who encounter barriers to stores, restaurants, and public buildings. They would lose the ability to go to court promptly and would have to wait out a notice-and-cure process of up to roughly six months, during which the business faces no penalty for keeping them out.

drawbacks.text: A person denied access to a public accommodation would have to wait through a 60-day notice period and then a 120-day cure period before they could sue, with no compensation or expedited relief during that time — meaning delayed access is simply access denied for months.

The standard that owners merely make 'substantial progress' after promising improvements is undefined in the bill, which could let owners repeatedly avoid a lawsuit by promising and partially delivering fixes for years.

Criminal fines for demand letters that omit required details could chill legitimate pre-suit notices, including ones from disabled people themselves describing real denials of access, shifting the balance of the ADA's enforcement system toward businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real problem on the demand-letter side: some letters are sent serially with vague allegations to extract settlements, and small businesses genuinely bear defense costs. The education and mediation programs are low-cost ideas most people could accept. But the core of the bill — the notice-and-cure period — trades away the ADA's main private enforcement tool, and disabled customers would pay for it in months of continued exclusion from places they cannot enter. The bill addresses the abuses with a remedy that delays the very access the ADA was written to guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 15-6 in July 2016, but House leaders never scheduled it for a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Poe introduced the bill on October 20, 2015, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Constitution and Civil Justice Subcommittee.
The bill sat in subcommittee for over eight months before being discharged on July 5, 2016, and the full Judiciary Committee held a markup on July 7, 2016.
At that markup the committee voted 15-6 to order the bill reported to the House with amendments.
No further action was taken: the bill was never reported to the full House or brought to a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with disabilities kept their existing right to go straight to court over inaccessible businesses, and owners of inaccessible premises never received the months of lawsuit protection and demand-letter immunity the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Disabled people who kept immediate court access

for.what_they_did: Held a markup on July 7, 2016 and voted 15-6 to order the bill reported as amended.

against.what_they_did: Opposed the notice-and-cure approach, arguing it delays access to public accommodations and weakens the ADA's private enforcement system.

sides.party_line_note: Support leaned Republican: 57 of the bill's 61 cosponsors were Republicans and 4 were Democrats, and no party breakdown of the 15-6 committee vote is recorded in the sources.

industries.industry: Commercial property owners and small businesses (retail, restaurants, services)
industries.note: The bill would give owners up to about 180 days of immunity from ADA lawsuits over barriers, plus criminal penalties for vague demand letters, while requiring no fix until after notice. The gain to owners comes directly at the cost of disabled customers who stay locked out during the waiting periods.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' firms filing ADA access suits
industries.note: Detailed-notice requirements backed by criminal fines and a mandatory pre-suit cure period would sharply limit demand-letter and lawsuit practice. The bill targets some genuinely abusive serial letters, but the same rules also curb legitimate claims by disabled people.

industries.industry: Access compliance consultants and Certified Access Specialists
industries.note: The Justice Department education program may include training for certified access specialists, creating paid work helping owners identify and fix barriers before anyone is excluded.
